name: Sarcosine (hair)

lead: Sarcosine is a small naturally occurring amino acid, an N-methyl form of glycine. It is listed as a component in some hair-growth blends, with the idea that it supports follicle energy and cells for fuller-looking hair.
In the body it is an intermediate in choline-to-glycine metabolism. No clinical study of sarcosine for hair growth was found.

paras: It is encountered as one listed ingredient in topical or supplement blends used as part of a regular hair routine.
No hair-specific safety data were described in the sources reviewed. Its sarcosinate derivatives are widely used as surfactants in consumer products.

lead: Sarcosine, also called N-methylglycine, is a non-proteinogenic amino acid that is the N-methyl derivative of glycine. It occurs naturally in muscle and other tissues as an intermediate in the conversion of choline to glycine.[1]

In appearance-related discussion it is mentioned as an ingredient in hair-growth blends. No published human study found in the sources reviewed has tested sarcosine itself as a hair-growth ingredient, so evidence for that use is unproven.

paras: Sarcosine (C3H7NO2) is a colourless, highly water-soluble crystalline solid that exists as a zwitterion at neutral pH. Justus von Liebig first isolated it in 1847. It is present in human blood at low micromolar levels.[1]

Sarcosine is used to make biodegradable surfactants such as sodium lauroyl sarcosinate, which appear in toothpaste and other products, and as a reagent in organic synthesis.[1] Research outside hair care has examined its action on the glycine transporter GlyT1 and NMDA receptors, with early studies in schizophrenia and rodent models of depression, and a debated role as a prostate cancer biomarker.[1]
No studies found. Studies of sarcosine in schizophrenia and other conditions exist but do not address hair growth or hair appearance.[1]
